name: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences
blurb: How drugmakers and biotechs adopt, govern, staff and pay for AI, and the tools they choose.
title: AI Adoption and Governance in Life Sciences
answer: Large drugmakers have moved from pilots to company wide AI programmes, often with a single primary partner: OpenAI with Moderna, Sanofi and Novo Nordisk, Microsoft and OpenAI tools at Amgen. The ones that report results tie AI to training, champions networks and governance rather than to tools alone.

reading.body:
Large drugmakers have moved from AI pilots to company wide programmes, and the ones reporting results tie adoption to training and governance, not to tools alone.

The pattern in the named cases is a single primary frontier partner rather than a spread of vendors. Moderna works with OpenAI, Sanofi with OpenAI and Formation Bio, Novo Nordisk with OpenAI, and Amgen with Microsoft and OpenAI tools. Each pairing is described as spanning the company rather than one function, which is a different kind of commitment from a departmental pilot.

What separates the companies that report results is organisational. Moderna set a proficiency goal for every eligible employee and built a network of internal champions. Amgen scaled its tools under measured testing and security review. In a regulated business the sequencing matters: decide which data each tool may see and which decisions it may touch before rollout, because governance constrains what the compute can be pointed at.

The data covers a small number of large drugmakers and their announced partnerships. It does not say how many employees use the tools daily, what the programmes cost, or whether they changed research or manufacturing outcomes. It also does not cover small biotechs, which may adopt very differently without the same governance apparatus.

sections.body: The companies reporting results treat AI as a change programme with executive ownership, training targets and named champions, not as a software purchase. Governance has to come first in a regulated business: decide which data each tool may see and which decisions it may touch before rollout.
sections.heading: What it means for a life sciences leader

explainer:
Adopting AI in a life sciences company is as much an organisational challenge as a technical one. These companies hold sensitive patient data, valuable intellectual property and regulated records, operate in many countries, and answer to inspectors who expect every system to be controlled. Rolling out AI to tens of thousands of employees has to work within that.

The largest drugmakers have moved past pilots. Several now give most staff access to enterprise AI assistants, have signed company wide agreements with frontier AI labs or cloud providers, and are building AI agents into research and commercial workflows. The ones that report measurable gains share a pattern: an executive owner, clear priorities, training tied to real tasks, networks of internal champions, and governance that decides in advance which data each tool may see and which decisions it may touch.

Failure follows the opposite pattern. Studies of AI projects find that most stall for organisational reasons, unclear goals, weak data and missing ownership, rather than because the model did not work. In regulated companies there is an added risk of shadow AI, staff using unapproved consumer tools with confidential data because approved ones are not available.

The practical sequence is governance first, then broad access with training, then targeted high value workflows, with results measured in business terms rather than usage counts.
key_points: Large drugmakers have moved from pilots to company wide AI programmes.
Successful programmes pair access with training, champions and executive ownership.
Most AI projects fail for organisational, not technical, reasons.
Shadow AI is a real risk where approved tools are missing.
Govern data and decisions before rollout, and measure business outcomes.
